# Introduction

The five largest metropolitan areas of India are Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata,
Chennai, and Bengaluru. These cities are on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the western
and eastern coasts, the Deccan plateau, and the Bay of Bengal. Each city has a
different pollution profile. Topography, industry, traffic, and climate have an
effect on this profile.

This article uses the `vayuayan` package to examine one question for all five
cities:

> **How does PM2.5 pollution change across the largest metros of India by
> season, by location, and by station coverage?**

We use two independent data sources:

- WUSTL ACAG V5GL04: satellite-derived PM2.5 at ~1 km resolution
- CPCB CAAQMS: ground-level readings from monitoring stations

The analysis has five parts:

1. When is pollution highest in each city? *(seasonal trends)*
2. How much does pollution change from day to day in each city? *(SD ribbons)*
3. How high is the annual pollution level of each city? *(cross-city ranking)*
4. Where in each city is pollution highest? *(spatial heatmaps)*
5. Do the cities have sufficient stations for their pollution burden? *(station coverage)*

---

# Data and methods

## Satellite data

The satellite data is the monthly PM2.5 estimates from WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 (~1 km
resolution, 1998 to 2022). The package uses a fast bounding-box subset method
to read the files. This method does not load the full 121 MB global array.

## Ground data

The ground data is city-level daily PM2.5 from the CPCB data repository.
`cpcb_download_city_data()` downloads this data. We calculate the monthly means
from the daily readings.

## Cities

| City      | Region         | CPCB Stations | Geography          |
|-----------|----------------|---------------|--------------------|
| Delhi     | North India    | 46            | Landlocked, IGP    |
| Mumbai    | West Coast     | 29            | Coastal peninsula  |
| Kolkata   | East India     | 7             | River delta, IGP   |
| Chennai   | South Coast    | 9             | Coastal, Bay       |
| Bengaluru | Deccan Plateau | 14            | Inland, elevated   |

## Comparison note

Ground readings are consistently higher than satellite estimates. The cause is a bias
in the locations of the stations near point sources (refer to the cross-city
ranking figure below). In this article, we use the same method to compare all
cities. Thus, the relative differences are correct, although the absolute values
from the two sources are different.

---

# Setup

```{r packages}
library(vayuayan)
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(tidyterra)
library(ncdf4)
library(khroma)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)
library(kableExtra)
library(here)
```

```{r folder-setup}
vignettes_dir <- here::here("vignettes")

data_dir <- file.path(vignettes_dir, "data/metro")
fig_dir <- file.path(vignettes_dir, "figures/metro")
for (d in c(data_dir, fig_dir)) {
  dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
}
```

## City configuration

```{r city-config}
cities <- list(
  Delhi     = list(name = "Delhi", color = "#c0392b"),
  Mumbai    = list(name = "Mumbai", color = "#2980b9"),
  Kolkata   = list(name = "Kolkata", color = "#8e44ad"),
  Chennai   = list(name = "Chennai", color = "#27ae60"),
  Bengaluru = list(name = "Bengaluru", color = "#e67e22")
)

city_names <- names(cities)
city_colors <- setNames(sapply(cities, `[[`, "color"), city_names)

extra_colors <- c(
  Surat     = "#e91e63",
  Kanpur    = "#9c27b0",
  Jaipur    = "#00bcd4",
  Lucknow   = "#3f51b5",
  Pune      = "#ff9800",
  Ahmedabad = "#cddc39",
  Hyderabad = "#ff5722"
)
all_colors <- c(city_colors, extra_colors)
extra_cities <- names(extra_colors)

# City boundaries are built from the BharatViz LGD district layer. Each city
# maps to one or more districts that are unioned together so that all CPCB
# stations fall within the boundary (e.g. Kolkata spans four districts,
# Hyderabad spans two). Delhi uses every district of the NCT.
city_districts <- list(
  Delhi = list(state = "Delhi"),
  Mumbai = list(district = c("Mumbai", "Mumbai Suburban")),
  Kolkata = list(district = c(
    "Kolkata", "24 Paraganas North", "24 Paraganas South", "Howrah"
  )),
  Chennai = list(district = "Chennai"),
  Bengaluru = list(district = "Bengaluru Urban"),
  Kanpur = list(district = "Kanpur Nagar"),
  Surat = list(district = "Surat"),
  Jaipur = list(district = "Jaipur"),
  Lucknow = list(district = "Lucknow"),
  Pune = list(district = "Pune"),
  Ahmedabad = list(district = "Ahmadabad"),
  Hyderabad = list(district = c("Hyderabad", "Ranga Reddy"))
)
```

```{r city-boundaries}
# india_boundary() unions the BharatViz districts (or all districts of a state,
# for Delhi) named in each city_districts entry.
city_shapes <- lapply(city_districts, do.call, what = india_boundary)
```

## Satellite reads

The satellite values come from WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 monthly files. The package
downloads these files one time from the AWS Open Data registry (Asia subset)
into `nc_dir`. `pm25_monthly()` gives the mean over the bounding box of a
region. `pm25_load_netcdf_bbox()` gives the cropped raster.

```{r nc-dir}
nc_dir <- file.path(vignettes_dir, "data/pm25")
```

---

# Results

## Seasonal trends

### Ground data: city-level monthly means

```{r ground-seasonal}
# Daily city readings for all 12 cities used in this article, one row per day.
# Files are cached in data_dir as <city>_aqi_2022.csv.
ground_daily <- cpcb_city_daily(c(city_names, extra_cities), 2022,
  cache_dir = data_dir
)

ground_monthly <- ground_daily %>%
  filter(city %in% city_names) %>%
  group_by(city, month) %>%
  summarise(
    ground_pm25 = mean(value),
    ground_sd   = sd(value),
    .groups     = "drop"
  )
```

### Satellite data: monthly spatial means

```{r satellite-seasonal}
sat_monthly <- city_shapes[city_names] %>%
  lapply(pm25_monthly, year = 2022, version = "V5GL04", region = "AS", cache_dir = nc_dir) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "city") %>%
  rename(sat_pm25 = pm25)

seasonal_combined <- ground_monthly %>%
  left_join(sat_monthly, by = c("city", "month"))
```

### Seasonal line chart

```{r seasonal-chart, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Monthly mean PM2.5 across five Indian metros, 2022. Solid lines are CPCB ground data. Dashed lines are WUSTL satellite estimates. Delhi has a very different pollution regime. Its winter peak is 3 to 5× higher than the peak of all other cities."}
ggplot(seasonal_combined, aes(x = month, color = city)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ground_pm25), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ground_pm25), size = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sat_pm25), linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 15, linetype = "dotted",
    color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 11.5, y = 23,
    label = "WHO 24hr (15)", size = 3, color = "grey40", hjust = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_color_manual(values = city_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = "India's metros: PM2.5 seasonal cycle (2022)",
    subtitle = "Solid = CPCB ground | Dashed = WUSTL satellite | Dotted = WHO 24hr guideline (15 µg/m³)",
    y        = expression(paste("PM2.5 (", mu, "g/m"^3, ")")),
    x        = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 + CPCB CAAQMS"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    text               = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position    = "top",
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9.5, color = "grey40")
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig1_metro_seasonal_comparison.png"), width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

> **Finding:** Delhi and Kolkata are on the Indo-Gangetic Plain. These two
> cities have the highest winter peaks. Sea breezes help the coastal cities
> (Mumbai, Chennai) through the full year. Pollution decreases in all cities
> during the monsoon. But only Bengaluru and Chennai come near safe levels in
> the wettest months.

---

### Day-to-day variability

The seasonal line chart shows monthly *means*. Means do not show the
day-to-day changes that residents experience. A city with a high mean and wide
variability is less predictable than a city with a constant moderate level.
Also, it is harder for residents to prepare for this type of city. The ribbon
below shows ±1 standard deviation around each monthly mean. We calculate the
standard deviation from the daily readings.

```{r seasonal-ribbon, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Day-to-day variability in monthly PM2.5 across five metros, 2022. The line is the monthly mean. The ribbon is ±1 SD across daily readings. Each city has its own Y-axis. The Delhi winter ribbon is very wide. It shows extreme pollution events in addition to a baseline that is already high."}
# Monthly mean and SD were computed in ground_monthly above
ground_monthly_sd <- ground_monthly %>%
  # Order facets by pollution level, most polluted first
  mutate(city = factor(city,
    levels = c(
      "Delhi", "Kolkata", "Mumbai",
      "Chennai", "Bengaluru"
    )
  ))

ggplot(
  ground_monthly_sd,
  aes(x = month, color = city, fill = city)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = ground_pm25 - ground_sd,
      ymax = ground_pm25 + ground_sd
    ),
    alpha = 0.15, color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ground_pm25), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ground_pm25), size = 2) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 15, linetype = "dotted",
    color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 1, y = 18,
    label = "WHO 24hr (15 µg/m³)",
    size = 2.8, color = "grey40", hjust = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_color_manual(values = city_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = city_colors, guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~city, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title    = "Day-to-day variability in monthly PM2.5: five metros (2022)",
    subtitle = "Line = monthly mean | Ribbon = ±1 SD across daily readings",
    y        = expression(paste("PM2.5 (", mu, "g/m"^3, ")")),
    x        = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: CPCB CAAQMS | 2022"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    text               = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position    = "none",
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9.5, color = "grey40")
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig1b_metro_seasonal_variability.png"),
  width = 10, height = 10, dpi = 300
)
```

> **Finding:** The Delhi winter ribbon is much wider than the ribbons of all
> other cities. The monthly mean and the day-to-day changes are extreme. A
> Delhi resident gets more pollution variability in one winter month than a
> Bengaluru resident gets in the full year.

---

## Cross-city ranking

Before we examine the spatial patterns, we compare the absolute values of the
cities. This step gives the reference for the heatmaps below.

```{r annual-summary}
annual_sat <- sat_monthly %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(annual_sat_pm25 = mean(sat_pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

annual_ground <- ground_monthly %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(annual_ground_pm25 = mean(ground_pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

winter_ground <- ground_monthly %>%
  filter(month %in% c(1, 10, 11, 12)) %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(winter_ground_pm25 = mean(ground_pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

who_exceedance <- ground_daily %>%
  filter(city %in% city_names) %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(
    who_exceed_days = sum(value > 15),
    total_days      = n(),
    .groups         = "drop"
  )

# Areas for all 12 cities in one call, in a metric projection
city_areas <- tibble(
  city = names(city_shapes),
  area_km2 = as.numeric(sf::st_area(
    sf::st_transform(do.call(c, city_shapes), 3857)
  )) / 1e6
)

station_data <- tibble(
  city       = c(city_names, extra_cities),
  n_stations = map_int(city, ~ nrow(cpcb_get_station_list(.x)))
)

city_summary <- station_data %>%
  filter(city %in% city_names) %>%
  left_join(city_areas, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(annual_sat, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(annual_ground, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(winter_ground, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(who_exceedance, by = "city") %>%
  mutate(
    stations_per_100km2 = round(n_stations / area_km2 * 100, 2),
    who_exceed_pct      = round(who_exceed_days / total_days * 100, 1)
  )
```

```{r rankings-bar, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Annual mean PM2.5 ranked across five Indian metros, 2022. All cities are more than the WHO 24-hour guideline of 15 µg/m³. The Delhi annual mean is many times the WHO limit."}
rankings <- city_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(annual_ground_pm25)) %>%
  mutate(
    annual_ground_pm25 = round(annual_ground_pm25, 1),
    annual_sat_pm25    = round(annual_sat_pm25, 1)
  )

rankings_long <- rankings %>%
  select(city, annual_ground_pm25, annual_sat_pm25) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(annual_ground_pm25, annual_sat_pm25),
    names_to = "source", values_to = "pm25"
  ) %>%
  mutate(source = recode(source,
    "annual_ground_pm25" = "CPCB Ground",
    "annual_sat_pm25"    = "WUSTL Satellite"
  ))

ggplot(
  rankings_long,
  aes(
    x = reorder(city, pm25), y = pm25,
    fill = city, alpha = source
  )
) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), width = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 15, linetype = "dotted",
    color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0.6, y = 18,
    label = "WHO 24hr (15 µg/m³)", size = 3,
    color = "grey40", hjust = 0
  ) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = city_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    values = c("CPCB Ground" = 0.95, "WUSTL Satellite" = 0.5),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Annual mean PM2.5: five Indian metros (2022)",
    subtitle = "Dark = CPCB ground | Light = WUSTL satellite | Dotted = WHO 24hr guideline",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = expression(paste("Annual mean PM2.5 (", mu, "g/m"^3, ")")),
    caption  = "Source: CPCB CAAQMS + WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 | 2022"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    text               = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
    legend.position    = "top"
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig2_metro_annual_ranking.png"), width = 10, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

> **Finding:** The Delhi annual mean is many times the annual mean of Mumbai,
> Chennai, and Bengaluru. The two data sources put the cities in the same
> sequence. Thus, the sequence is reliable, although the
> absolute values are different. All five cities are more than the WHO
> guidelines each year.

---

## Spatial heatmaps

The annual means show *how much* pollution each city has. The heatmaps show
*where* the pollution is highest in each city. Each city uses an independent
color scale. Thus, the spatial structure in each city is clear.

We put the cities in two groups by geography. The Indo-Gangetic Plain cities
(Delhi, Kolkata, Kanpur) have the same pollution cause: the IGP trap. The
coastal and southern cities (Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru) are the other group.

```{r heatmap-data}
# IGP group (Delhi, Kolkata, Kanpur) and coastal/southern group (Mumbai,
# Chennai, Bengaluru), using the BharatViz boundaries in city_shapes.
heatmap_cities <- c("Delhi", "Kolkata", "Kanpur", "Mumbai", "Chennai", "Bengaluru")
nov_file <- pm25_download_netcdf(2022, 11, version = "V5GL04", region = "AS", cache_dir = nc_dir)

# November raster for each city, cropped and masked to its boundary
nov_rasters <- lapply(city_shapes[heatmap_cities], pm25_load_netcdf_bbox,
  nc_path = nov_file, mask = TRUE
)

# pm25_map() draws each raster on its own 2nd to 98th percentile colour scale
heatmap_theme <- theme(
  text              = element_text(family = "Arial"),
  legend.position   = "right",
  legend.key.width  = unit(0.4, "lines"),
  legend.key.height = unit(3, "lines"),
  legend.text       = element_text(size = 7),
  plot.title        = element_text(size = 11),
  plot.subtitle     = element_text(size = 9)
)
heatmaps <- Map(pm25_map, nov_rasters, city_shapes[heatmap_cities], heatmap_cities) %>%
  lapply(`+`, heatmap_theme)
```

```{r heatmaps-igp, fig.width=12, fig.height=5, fig.cap="November 2022 PM2.5 in Indo-Gangetic Plain cities (Delhi, Kolkata, Kanpur). All three cities are in the IGP pollution trap. Each city uses its own color scale. For absolute values, refer to Figure 2."}
wrap_plots(heatmaps[c("Delhi", "Kolkata", "Kanpur")], ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "IGP cities: Delhi · Kolkata · Kanpur",
    subtitle = "Indo-Gangetic Plain, November 2022 | Per-city color scale | Source: WUSTL ACAG V5GL04",
    caption = "Scales are not comparable across panels. Refer to Figure 2 for cross-city absolute comparison",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
      plot.caption  = element_text(size = 9, color = "firebrick", face = "italic")
    )
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig3a_heatmaps_igp.png"), width = 13, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

> **IGP finding:** All three cities have higher values in northern/western
> areas, where pollution collects against the terrain. Kanpur has lower absolute
> values than Delhi. But the industrial belt of Kanpur along the Ganga causes
> strong spatial gradients.

```{r heatmaps-coastal, fig.width=12, fig.height=5, fig.cap="November 2022 PM2.5 in coastal and southern cities (Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru). Sea breezes and elevation give these cities structurally lower pollution. Spatial gradients show industrial and traffic hotspots."}
wrap_plots(heatmaps[c("Mumbai", "Chennai", "Bengaluru")], ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Coastal and southern cities: Mumbai · Chennai · Bengaluru",
    subtitle = "November 2022 | Per-city color scale | Source: WUSTL ACAG V5GL04",
    caption = "Scales are not comparable across panels. Refer to Figure 2 for cross-city absolute comparison",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
      plot.caption  = element_text(size = 9, color = "firebrick", face = "italic")
    )
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig3b_heatmaps_coastal.png"), width = 13, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

> **Coastal finding:** The peninsular shape of Mumbai causes a clear east-west
> gradient. The eastern industrial suburbs (Thane, Navi Mumbai corridor) always
> have consistently higher PM2.5 than the western seafront. Chennai and Bengaluru
> have more diffuse patterns, because their industry is less concentrated.

---

## Station coverage

A city with many stations can have bad station coverage if all the stations
are in one area. This section examines 12 Indian cities. We examine if the
investment in stations agrees with the pollution burden.

```{r extra-cities}
# Daily readings for the extra cities were downloaded into ground_daily above.
# Hyderabad combines Hyderabad + Ranga Reddy (the full GHMC metro area) through
# its multi-district mapping in city_districts.
extra_ground <- ground_daily %>%
  filter(city %in% extra_cities) %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(annual_ground_pm25 = mean(value), .groups = "drop")

extra_summary <- station_data %>%
  filter(city %in% extra_cities) %>%
  left_join(city_areas, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(extra_ground, by = "city") %>%
  mutate(stations_per_100km2 = round(n_stations / area_km2 * 100, 2))

all_city_summary <- bind_rows(
  city_summary %>% select(
    city, n_stations, area_km2,
    annual_ground_pm25, stations_per_100km2
  ),
  extra_summary
)

write.csv(all_city_summary, file.path(data_dir, "all_city_summary.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r summary-table}
tbl_data <- all_city_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(annual_ground_pm25)) %>%
  mutate(
    area_km2            = round(area_km2, 0),
    annual_ground_pm25  = round(annual_ground_pm25, 1),
    stations_per_100km2 = round(stations_per_100km2, 3)
  ) %>%
  select(
    City                   = city,
    `Stations`             = n_stations,
    `Area (km²)`           = area_km2,
    `Annual PM2.5 (µg/m³)` = annual_ground_pm25,
    `Stations per 100 km²` = stations_per_100km2
  )

tbl_data %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Table 1: CPCB monitoring station density across 12 Indian cities (2022). Cities ranked by annual mean PM2.5. Red values in the last column indicate near-zero station density (<0.05 per 100 km²). These cities have the fewest stations for their area.",
    align   = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    format  = "html"
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width        = FALSE,
    position          = "center"
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(
    5,
    bold  = TRUE,
    color = ifelse(tbl_data$`Stations per 100 km²` < 0.05, "red", "black")
  )
```

```{r density-scatter, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Station density vs annual mean PM2.5 across 12 Indian cities, 2022. Cities in the top-left (high PM2.5, low station density) have the least monitoring for their pollution burden. The Y-axis has a log scale."}
median_pm25 <- median(all_city_summary$annual_ground_pm25, na.rm = TRUE)
median_density <- median(all_city_summary$stations_per_100km2, na.rm = TRUE)

all_city_summary <- all_city_summary %>%
  mutate(
    quadrant = case_when(
      annual_ground_pm25 >= median_pm25 &
        stations_per_100km2 < median_density ~ "High pollution\nLow coverage",
      annual_ground_pm25 >= median_pm25 &
        stations_per_100km2 >= median_density ~ "High pollution\nGood coverage",
      annual_ground_pm25 < median_pm25 &
        stations_per_100km2 < median_density ~ "Low pollution\nLow coverage",
      TRUE ~ "Low pollution\nGood coverage"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  all_city_summary,
  aes(x = stations_per_100km2, y = annual_ground_pm25, color = city)
) +
  # Quadrant shading
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = -Inf, xmax = median_density,
    ymin = median_pm25, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#d6604d", alpha = 0.06
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = median_density * 0.1, y = max(all_city_summary$annual_ground_pm25) * 0.95,
    label = "Under-monitored\n(high PM2.5, low density)",
    size = 3, color = "#d6604d", hjust = 0, fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median_density, linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = median_pm25, linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 5, alpha = 0.85) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = city),
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    box.padding = 0.6,
    point.padding = 0.4,
    show.legend = FALSE,
    max.overlaps = 20
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = all_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title    = "Monitoring coverage vs pollution burden: 12 Indian cities (2022)",
    subtitle = "Top-left = under-monitored | Dashed lines = median values | Y axis log scale",
    x        = "CPCB stations per 100 km²",
    y        = expression(paste("Annual mean PM2.5 (", mu, "g/m"^3, ")")),
    caption  = "Source: CPCB CAAQMS + WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 | 2022"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    text             = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
    plot.caption     = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey50")
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "fig4_metro_station_density.png"), width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

> **Finding:** Some cities with very high pollution are in the under-monitored
> quadrant. This quadrant has high PM2.5 and low station density. This
> combination is the worst. The cities that must have the most stations have the
> smallest coverage.

---

# Discussion

## Day-to-day variability

The SD ribbon plots show that pollution in Delhi has a high mean and is very
unpredictable. The Delhi winter ribbon is much wider than the ribbons of all
other cities. Thus, residents of Delhi get extreme day-to-day changes in air
quality. The coastal cities have thin ribbons through the full year. Their
pollution is lower and more predictable.

This unpredictability has an effect on health. Residents cannot accurately
prepare for outdoor exposure, although they know that winter is usually bad.

## Geography and seasonal patterns

The seasonal analysis shows that geography has a large effect on pollution
patterns. Delhi and Kolkata are on the Indo-Gangetic Plain. These two cities
have the highest winter peaks. Sea breezes give some ventilation to the coastal
cities (Mumbai, Chennai) through the full year.

The geography of the IGP makes a trap for pollutants. The Himalayas stop the
cold northern winds that can move pollutants away. Shallow temperature
inversions keep emissions near the surface.

## The monsoon and pollution levels

In all five cities, pollution decreases during the southwest monsoon (June to
September). But pollution decreases by very different quantities in the
different cities. In Delhi, monsoon PM2.5 stays above the WHO annual limit.
Chennai and Bengaluru come near safe levels in the wettest months. These two
cities have lower baseline emissions. Also, rain removes a larger part of the
pollutants from the air of these two cities.

## Spatial heterogeneity within cities

The per-city heatmaps show that pollution is not the same in all areas of a
city. The IGP
cities (Delhi, Kolkata, Kanpur) have strong northern and western gradients,
where pollutants collect against terrain features. The coastal cities have
different patterns. In Mumbai, the industrial eastern suburbs cause an east-west
gradient. Chennai and Bengaluru have more diffuse distributions, because their
industry is less concentrated. In all cities, city-level means show less
exposure than the residents of the most polluted neighborhoods get.

## Monitoring coverage

The station density analysis shows that the investment in stations does not
always agree with the pollution burden. The 12-city scatter plot shows that many
large, polluted cities have a much smaller number of stations than their
pollution burden makes necessary. The cities where measurement is most
necessary frequently have the smallest coverage.

---

# Limitations

- SD ribbons: The ±1 SD ribbon is correct only for approximately symmetrical
  distributions. PM2.5 is usually right-skewed. Thus, on clean days, the lower
  bound of the ribbon can go below possible values. Use the ribbon only to see
  the approximate spread. Do not use the ribbon as a strict confidence
  interval.

- Satellite data version: V5GL04 has data for 1998 to 2022. When V6GL02 is
  available, you can use the same method for all years.

- Independent heatmap scales: Per-city color scales show the spatial structure
  in each city. You cannot use these scales to compare absolute pollution
  levels between cities. To compare absolute values between cities, use
  Figure 2. To make the heatmaps easier to read, we put the cities in two
  geographic groups: IGP (Delhi, Kolkata, Kanpur) and coastal/southern (Mumbai,
  Chennai, Bengaluru).

- City boundary files: The results change with the definition of the city
  boundaries. Administrative boundaries can be different from the functional
  urban area where pollution occurs and where stations measure it.

- Station count only: This analysis counts stations. The analysis does not
  examine the spatial distribution of the stations in each city.

- 2022 only: One year can be different from the long-term pollution
  climatology. Year-to-year variability can cause large changes in the annual
  means. The variability in monsoon intensity is an important example.

- Boundary source: We make the city boundaries from the BharatViz LGD district
  layer (`geo.bharatviz.org`). Each city boundary is the union of one or more
  districts. Delhi uses all districts of the NCT.

- Kolkata boundary: The boundary includes four districts (Kolkata, 24 Paraganas
  North, 24 Paraganas South, Howrah). Thus, all 7 CPCB stations are in the
  boundary.

- Hyderabad boundary: The boundary includes the Hyderabad and Ranga Reddy
  districts (~8,500 km²). The Hyderabad district without Ranga Reddy
  (~197 km²) has the administrative boundaries from before the GHMC
  expansion.
